lesson_text: A drop of 10% to 20% from the high. That's the line most people use. More than 10% off the peak is a correction, and 20% or more is a bear market. Alan Shaw, one of the founders of technical analysis, gave us these labels. Anything under 10% he called a consolidation. Don't treat the lines as laws though. Schwab says no definition is universally accepted, and Morningstar calls the 10% line arbitrary. They're a quick way to say how deep the damage is. Know them so you read the headlines right, then get back to your charts. More than 10% off the high is a correction. 20% or more is a bear market.

answer_json.answer: A few weeks to a few months

lesson_text: A few weeks to a few months. Dow Theory sorts moves by size. The big one is the primary trend, the bull or bear market itself, running a few months to many years. Inside it you get the secondary move, the pullback against that trend. In a bull market that's your correction, and it runs a few weeks to a few months. Below that sits the daily noise, hours to days, rarely past a week. Morningstar's average correction of three to four months lands right in that window. So a few weeks of selling inside a bull doesn't tell me the bull is over. I keep my list ready and watch which names hold up best. A correction runs against the trend for weeks or months. The main trend runs months to years.

answer_json.answer: A sharp drop on unusually heavy volume

lesson_text: The sharp drop on unusually heavy volume. That's panic, everyone heading for the exit at once. On the chart it's a wide red bar with volume way above normal. Often price closes well off the low that day, because big buyers are soaking up the selling. That's the look of a washout. I mark that day's low. I'm not buying it yet. I want to see what happens when price comes back to test it. Big drop, huge volume, a close well off the low. That's the look of a washout.

answer_json.answer: How many stocks join a move

lesson_text: How many stocks join the move. That's all breadth is. The index tells you how far it went. Breadth tells you how many came along. So a green SPY with a red watchlist isn't in your head. A few big gainers can carry the index while most stocks sit it out. Breadth isn't volume. Some gauges add volume, but the core is a count of stocks. And it isn't market depth either, which is how much size the market takes without moving the price. The index tells you how far. Breadth tells you how many came along.

answer_json.answer: A known Nasdaq quirk, not a crash call

lesson_text: A known Nasdaq quirk, not a crash call. Nasdaq's listing standards are looser than the NYSE's. So more companies that end up failing list there, and every one of them piles onto the declines. Its A/D line has drifted down since its data began in 1972 and never got back. It even fell from 2010 to 2012 while the Nasdaq rose. McClellan called the June 2024 picture not unusual. So for divergence reads, I lean on the NYSE line. Don't read the Nasdaq A/D line like the NYSE's. It can fall for long stretches while the index rises.

sources.quote: The Advance-Decline Line (AD Line) is a breadth indicator based on Net Advances, which is the number of advancing stocks less the number of declining stocks. … The AD Line is a cumulative measure of Net Advances, rising when it is positive and falling when it is negative. … An AD Line that rises and records new highs along with the underlying index shows strong participation that is bullish. … An AD Line that fails to keep pace with the underlying index and confirm new highs shows narrowing participation. … Narrowing participation is often identified with a bearish divergence between the AD Line and the underlying index. … Chart 3 shows two bearish divergences in the NYSE AD Line from June to November 2007. sources.quote: For short-to-medium-term timeframes, it's helpful to look at the percentage of stocks trading above the 50-day moving average. … The calculation is straightforward: divide the number of stocks above their XX-day moving average by the total number of stocks in the underlying index. … A bullish bias is present when the indicator is above 50%. lesson_text: It turns into a market order and sells. Your 6% stop is a trigger, not a promised price. SPY opened 5.2% down, then traded through your 6% line within minutes, so the order went to market. In a fast open it takes whatever's there, and that could be near the 7.8% low. By 9:40 SPY was back above its open, and it closed down only 4.2%. So the stop could have sold you within a hair of the worst print of the day. That's why, when a big gap down opens near my stop, I handle it by hand. The low of the first half hour becomes my new stop. If that low takes the loss past twice what I planned to risk, I'm out. A stop is a trigger, not a price. In a wild open it can sell you near the low.

It becomes a market order and sells

lesson_text: Stocks can slide while the economy grows. The 2001 recession ended in November 2001, and the economy kept growing through 2002. Stocks fell anyway. Accounting scandals, profit warnings and tension abroad drove the slide. By early October, indexes sat at their lowest since spring 1997. They turned in late October, when third-quarter earnings came in better than feared. In 2009 stocks bottomed before the recession ended. Here they bottomed almost a year after it ended. Two different clocks. So don't use the economy to time the market. Read the chart in front of you. The economy and the market keep different clocks. Trade the chart, not the GDP headlines.

lesson_text: Demand holds up when the economy slows. People keep buying toothpaste, power and prescription drugs in a recession, so those companies' profits stay steadier. Here's the part people miss. Defensive doesn't mean the stock goes up when the market drops. In 2022, with dividends, staples still lost 0.70% while the S&P 500 lost 18.11%. They fell less. They still fell. And it has nothing to do with debt. Plenty of utilities borrow heavily. Defensive means steady demand. It doesn't mean the stock goes up in a selloff.

depth.summary: Late in the cycle, energy and utility stocks have done well as inflation rises. In the textbook model, materials and energy show relative strength near the market's top. Sector rotation analysis compares the eleven sector funds' relative performance and links it to the business cycle. No investment has behaved the same way in every cycle. A cycle is easy to identify after it ends and hard to call while it's happening. StockCharts describes its business cycle as the ideal one for an inflationary environment. Cycle phases have varied widely in length. Wyckoff's method: first find a group with relative strength, then the strong stocks inside it. Some groups lead the market and some lag it, even though the market sets the overall trend. Buy relative strength and avoid relative weakness. Our rule C31: buy leaders, in one of the strongest groups.

wrong.Drop sectors, trade the stock alone: Groups still lead and lag the market. Use the model for where to look, then let strength confirm it.
